stances.claim: The Annex on Power Sharing of FAB is a significant milestone but its 16-month gestation was characterized by birth pains because the most difficult part of any negotiation with secessionist undertones is determining what powers to cede -- rebels don't recognize the Constitution, but government negotiators are duty-bound to it, on pain of SC strike-down.

The PH negotiators were careful to word the FAB and its annexes to avoid any grant of independence or right of secession -- avoiding the Machakos South Sudan (referendum-for-self-determination), Good Friday Northern Ireland (referendum-to-secede-to-Ireland), and 1965 Malaysia-Singapore (separation) models -- recognizing instead the sovereignty of the Philippines, its Constitution, and its legal processes.

The annex's three-power categorization (Reserved + Concurrent + Exclusive) and ministerial-Bangsamoro-government structure resembles a federalized parliamentary government like Malaysia (the official facilitator of the MILF peace process) -- and harmonizing this with the PH's centralized presidential system will be a hurdle, both conceptually in drafting the basic law and practically in implementing it.

That the basic law must be passed by Congress connotes Constitutional supremacy (a refreshing departure from the Sudanese and Irish peace models that resulted in South Sudan becoming an independent state that eventually declared war on Sudan) -- and means any constitutional challenge to the FAB and its annexes may be premature until BBL passage and Presidential approval, because it is the basic law that will create and govern Bangsamoro, not the FAB and its annexes.

Per Dean Sedfrey Candelaria (FLP Professorial Chair holder), 'a peace agreement, no matter how well crafted, remains vulnerable to the constant test of public scrutiny at every stage of its implementation' -- and a deeper study is needed to intertwine the two contrasting types of democratic governance if cherished peace must endure.

notable_anecdotes: Coronel-Ferrer's birth-pains metaphor -- 'laborious document carried in our wombs for 16 months, and after the labor pains, we heaved our collective sigh of relief' -- among the most vivid negotiator's quotes in the CJP peace-process columns.

The three-foreign-peace-model contrast (Machakos South Sudan + Good Friday Northern Ireland + 1965 Malaysia-Singapore) -- concise comparative-constitutional precedent-handling that anchors the constitutional-supremacy argument.

The cautionary tale about South Sudan -- 'an independent South Sudan that eventually declared war on Sudan, its parent-state' -- used as the punchline of why PH chose the constitutional-supremacy path rather than the referendum path.

The federalized-parliamentary-with-Malaysia-as-facilitator-irony observation -- Malaysia, whose government structure is being replicated in Bangsamoro, is also the official facilitator of the MILF peace process -- a sharp comparative-institutional insight.
Dean Candelaria's quoted aphorism on peace-agreement vulnerability to public-scrutiny at every stage of implementation -- a Professorial Chair holder's epigram CJP folds into his FLP-aligned closing.

The 'May our people be gifted with lasting peace as the New Year dawns' closing -- among CJP's seasonal closings in his December columns, here applied to a peace process rather than a Catholic-liturgical context.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the Dec 8 2013 signing of the Annex on Power Sharing of the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro (FAB) as a significant milestone in the elusive search for lasting peace with the MILF. Prof. Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, the Philippine peace-panel chair, described the 'laborious document' as carried 'in our wombs' for 16 months, with collective relief after the labor pains. He explains the structural difficulty of any negotiation with secessionist undertones: rebels do not recognize the legitimacy of the government or the Constitution overarching it, so their demands are not constrained by the Charter, while government negotiators are duty-bound to it -- on pain of SC strike-down, as in North Cotabato v. Republic (Oct 14 2008), which voided the GMA-administration MOA-AD with the MILF. He observes that the PH negotiators were careful to word the FAB and its annexes to avoid any implication of independence or secession -- they did not include anything similar to the Machakos Agreement (2002), which gave South Sudan the right to self-determination through referendum; nor the Good Friday Agreement (1998), which provided that upon a referendum Northern Ireland may secede from the UK and join Ireland; nor the 1965 Malaysia-Singapore separation. Instead the FAB recognizes the sovereignty of the Philippines, its Constitution, and its legal processes. The annex delineates three governmental power categories: Reserved Powers (retained by the Central Government), Concurrent Powers (shared), and Exclusive Powers (Bangsamoro). The Bangsamoro government will be ministerial in structure, headed by a chief minister elected by a Bangsamoro Assembly of at least 50 members -- a federalized-parliamentary-government structure akin to Malaysia (which is by the way the official facilitator of the MILF peace process). That the basic law must be passed by Congress connotes Constitutional supremacy -- a refreshing departure from the Sudanese and Irish models, the former having resulted in an independent South Sudan that eventually declared war on Sudan, its parent-state -- and means any constitutional challenge to the FAB and its annexes may be premature until the Bangsamoro Basic Law (BBL) is passed by Congress and approved by the President, because it is the BBL that will create and govern the Bangsamoro. He flags the harmonization hurdle: how to fit a ministerial-federalized-parliamentary Bangsamoro government inside the PH's centralized presidential system, both conceptually in the BBL and practically in implementation. Citing Dean Sedfrey Candelaria (CJP Professorial Chair on Liberty and Prosperity), 'a peace agreement, no matter how well crafted, remains vulnerable to the constant test of public scrutiny at every stage of its implementation.' He looks forward to the fourth and last annex on normalization (Ferrer's February forecast) and closes: May our people be gifted with lasting peace as the New Year dawns.
